Hexham bus station parking charges introduced as flats plan revived

15th October
Local government
Planning and development
Hexham
Northumberland
By Natalie Finnigan Reporter

Share

0 comments
Read More

as Hallstile Bank partially reopens

NEW parking charges have been introduced at Hexham’s former bus station as the owner revives plans to build apartments on part of the long-derelict site.

The Priestpopple car park, owned by Dysart Group, was previously available for free under a temporary agreement with Northumberland County Council.

Charges now start at 99p for two hours, rising to £1.99 for four hours, £2.99 for six hours, £3.99 for 12 hours and £5.99 for 24 hours. Cashless payments can be made through PayByPhone or RingGo.

Dysart says it is preparing plans for town centre apartments on part of the site, although no detailed proposals or timetable have been announced.

The new parking charges introduced at the former bus station site on Priestpopple, Hexham (Image: Shaun Cosgrove)

The former bus station closed in 2016 following the completion of a £2.28 million replacement close to Hexham Hospital. Dysart Developments subsequently acquired the site, but its plans for a mixed-use development, including over 30 apartments, never materialised.

Mike Clark, development director at the Dysart Group, said: "Although we offered to extend the previous arrangement with the council providing free car parking under licence to them, which had lasted for several years and I think has been well received by users, the council decided that it no longer wanted to offer free parking at the bus station.

"We are currently preparing a development for part of the site to deliver town centre apartments, but as this will take several months to mobilise, I’ve agreed to maintain car parking temporarily over that period.

"We will have to levy a charge to cover insurance and costs, and it is only a temporary arrangement, but hopefully well received for the Christmas period."

Mr Clark said he hoped to see a “vibrant and active town centre” and recognised that convenient parking remained a significant issue for market towns such as Hexham.

“I hope we will be able to help by regenerating the site and helping sustain the town centre," Mr Clark said.

A spokesperson for Northumberland County Council said: "We are proud of our free parking offer in our town centres, including in Hexham, and we're one of the very few councils that continue to provide this.

"This was a temporary arrangement with a private landowner some time ago while we completed our new 250-space car park at nearby Alemouth Road.

"We terminated this licence in summer 2025, saving the council and taxpayers the cost of the business rates which it had been paying for the site."

Derek Kennedy, mayor of Hexham, welcomed plans for the site.

Cllr Kennedy said: "After many years, it’s good to read that Dysart plans to construct some development on the old bus station site.

"This bombsite has been a blight on our town for a decade, when the original plans were circulated.

"The use of the old bus station as a temporary car park was useful, but we were surprised that charging has been introduced.

"We do hope the site is developed and contributes to the health, commerce and sustainability of the town."

Suzanne Fairless-Aitken, county councillor for Hexham East, said she was "surprised" to learn of the changes to the bus station site.

Cllr Fairless-Aitken said: "As ward councillor for Hexham East, who's been campaigning for the bus station to be cleaned up and developed, rather than look like the neglected rubbish dump that it is, I'm somewhat surprised, firstly, to have not been told anything about this new change in planning from Northumberland County Council, and secondly, that a paid-for car park has been allowed to go ahead when there are strict planning rules on parking sites within a conservation area, such as screening measures.

"However, what is good is that this move appears to be a temporary measure before a build, and that some sort of planning for apartments in the town centre is now in the offing - but I have been told this by both Northumberland County Council and Dysart for the last five years I have been elected - and there's still nothing.

The Wombles serving the 215 notice in 2024 (Image: Supplied)

"It would be good to have a projected timeline for this.

"Hopefully, Dysart will now fill in the potholes, stop cars parking onto the marked footway and regularly clear away all the rubbish that has been part of this decade-long Hexham eyesore," she added.

Cllr Trevor Cessford, who represents Hexham North, said he had been informed almost two years ago by Northumberland County Council’s strategic estates manager that the authority’s use of the site for parking was coming to an end, following the creation of 250 free spaces at the Bunker Site.

He added: “In the interim, NCC had been paying for the use of the old bus station for extra free parking.

“Now this has ended, Dysart has decided to keep the parking in the short term before they develop the site, hopefully in the very near future, and they have made the decision to charge to park there to offset their costs.

“As it’s private land, they are well within their rights to do that. All council-owned parking will still remain free; some is time-limited, some all day.”
